    {
      "startEvent": 676,
      "endEvent": 689,
      "contextStartEvent": 619,
      "contextEndEvent": 828,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "we're living on borrowed time and in danger of running out of it",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["fear"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The borrowed-time affirmation answers successful secular societies by treating their stability as residual religion. Peterson supplies an inherited-ethics explanation at E690–704 and distinguishes religious dimensions at E759–794. Those reasons do not establish inevitable depletion, but the passage does not explicitly make every future secular success irrelevant."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 899,
      "endEvent": 907,
      "contextStartEvent": 861,
      "contextEndEvent": 929,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "serves in your psychological hierarchy as your equivalent of God",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Peterson reinterprets gratitude without a specified recipient as having a functional God-equivalent. The missing bridge concerns why diffuse gratitude occupies that hierarchical role. This is an ordinary conditional argument, not a substitute catchphrase. Blackmore disputes the equivalence at E908–915; whether Peterson's definition excludes her distinction regardless of merits remains unclear."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1073,
      "endEvent": 1092,
      "contextStartEvent": 1044,
      "contextEndEvent": 1139,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "most of the people who claim to be atheists aren't",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The affirmation challenges atheists' self-description through their conduct. Peterson offers fictional moral psychology at E1076–1128 and applies it to Blackmore's writing at E1129–1133, leaving the bridge from ethical action to religious belief disputed. He explicitly limits the claim to most atheists; reasoning is present, and comprehensive immunity to objections is not established."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1153,
      "endEvent": 1168,
      "contextStartEvent": 1134,
      "contextEndEvent": 1245,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "you're acting out the culture of the book",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After Blackmore's objection, Peterson again identifies her writing with religious activity. He supplies cultural inheritance and embodied-motivation arguments at E1154–1164 and E1235–1245, but does not establish why these make her an implicit believer. His functional usage may explain the disagreement; it is unclear whether it protects a substantive religious claim regardless of evidence."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1279,
      "endEvent": 1286,
      "contextStartEvent": 1264,
      "contextEndEvent": 1288,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "but it doesn't matter because it's God for you",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Peterson explicitly makes inability to name or believe in this God irrelevant to possessing it at E1281–1286. That protects his attribution against those objections. However, E1273–1281 defines God functionally as the highest value and supplies an action-based rationale; the affirmation summarizes that argument rather than replacing it with an unsupported slogan."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 481,
      "endEvent": 489,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "I'm not necessarily even saying that they're successful antidotes",
      "explanation": "Peterson distinguishes stories' proposed function from demonstrated effectiveness. E465–480 supplies his tragedy-to-malevolence rationale, while E485–489 expressly leaves their success open."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 945,
      "endEvent": 987,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "this is how the world is get used to it",
      "explanation": "The compact affirmation describes personal coping. When challenged, Blackmore supplies bodily needs and ordinary motivation as reasons action can continue without ultimate purpose at E954–987; E995–998 further distinguishes constructed meanings."
    }
  ]
